newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-UEFA SET UP CASH FUND TO HELP SMALLER CLUBS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UEFA SET UP CASH FUND TO HELP SMALLER CLUBS.

text.p: UEFA are to establish a fund to provide compensation to amateur and smaller professional clubs when they lose their best players to bigger clubs without a transfer fee being paid.

The decision, taken by UEFA's executive committee on Wednesday is sure to be welcomed by smaller clubs throughout Europe whose survival has been under some threat since the Bosman ruling of December 1995.
Part of the ruling did away with the payment for a player's transfer if he was at the end of his contract.
Those transfers were the lifeblood of many smaller clubs whose futures will be greatly helped, if not guaranteed, by UEFA's decision.

Executive committee member Jean Fournet-Fayard of France said on Wednesday: "We are looking at a figure of a maximum 150,000 Swiss francs ($105,000) to go to the amateur club or smaller club from a pool established by money from TV revenue.

"This pool is aimed at helping the smaller clubs. When players move across borders from an amateur to a professional club there is no transfer fee involved at present when the players have finished their contracts."

UEFA spokesman Mick Michels added: "This situation is also now affecting transfers between clubs in the same country so UEFA has set up this new fund to guarantee the security of the smaller clubs. It is not a transfer fee as such, but compensation."

In December 1995, the European Union ruled that soccer players were entitled to the same freedom of movement as other EU workers at the end of their contracts and clubs could not charge a transfer fee for letting them leave.
The ruling followed a five-year legal fight by the Belgian player Jean-Marc Bosman.
Since then UEFA has examined the ways in which smaller clubs under its jurisdiction could be protected from the serious implications inherent in that ruling.
At their meeting in Tenerife last December UEFA took an idea borrowed from the French system which guaranteed young players at smaller clubs long contracts until the age of 24.
This was designed to help smaller clubs keep their best young players for a number of years and receive full compensation if they left before the end of their contract.
The EU did not accept that idea as a basis for pan-European-wide transfers, but it seems possible that UEFA's latest proposal should prove more acceptable to Brussels.
